done.why: I swam into the lake with the lantern on me and it was ruined ("it will not light again"). Without light every room between the stair and anywhere useful was pitch black, so I kept getting eaten by grues. The fourth death put me in the Void for good. I'd still found only a small part of the world.

about: You're at the bottom of an endless stair, the last test set by an old man who says he's waiting for you. You pull a sword's worth of courage out of a rock, fight a hooded figure who turns out to wear your own face, and take its hood and cloak instead of killing it. Then you dive into a freezing lake for an amulet, picking up the old man's regalia piece by piece. It's about the ruins of a fallen Empire and earning your worth, and about how one careless step can cost you the light you need for everything else.

ending.what: A losing ending. After my fourth death (a grue, in the dark, once my lantern was waterlogged) a voice said "perhaps it has been another that I have been seeking" and left me in the Void, where "nothing further will happen to you in this game."

moments.note: The lantern is described as an old friend from two earlier adventures, and the tone is warm and a little rueful.
The sword won't come out of the rock, which is fair, but I got no clue about what would free it.
The hooded figure appeared and the sword from the junction jumped into my hand by itself. That was a great reveal.
Three hits in a row left me one wound from death before I understood the fight.
Jumping at the aqueduct killed me, but I woke in a prison-cell vision of the old man and then back at the stair. Death was forgiving here, and it was beautifully written.
I unhooded the beaten figure and saw my own face turn into an old man's. The best moment of the game.
"hello sailor" at the ocean got "Nothing happens yet." The "yet" pulled me in, but nothing ever came.
Entering the lake made me drop everything I was carrying, with no warning.
The shiny object slipped out of my hand. Picking it up seemed to be random.
The lamp stopped working because it got wet. I didn't know yet that this was permanent.
I walked north into the dark and a grue killed me. I lost the cloak, hood and amulet I'd worked for.
"it will not light again." With no light the game was effectively over.
RESTART is refused in character. That was clever, but it trapped me.
The fourth death was final, and the Void is a closed, quiet ending.

wished: Some warning or a way out before the lake ruined the only light source, or a way to dry or repair the lamp
Finding the other ways out of the Junction and the Barren Area: the east rubble, the northwest slide, the mist to the west
Seeing whatever the ocean's "Nothing happens yet" was building toward
Getting across to the south and west shores of the lake
Doing something with the crumbling aqueduct pillar the text kept hinting at
Starting over after I'd soft-locked myself

lines.line: It has the look of an old friend who has followed you somewhere it would rather not have come.
lines.why: It made the lantern feel like a character, which made losing it hurt.

lines.line: You slowly remove the hood from your badly wounded opponent and recoil in horror at the sight of your own face, weary and wounded.
lines.why: This was the emotional peak. The fight turned out to be about me.

lines.line: It is the saddest thing you have seen underground, and you have seen some sad things.
lines.why: The aqueduct's mournfulness gave the place a history.

lines.line: It will take a thinner day than this one.
lines.why: A charming way to say no to an exit.

lines.line: there is water behind the glass and a smell of wet metal, and it will not light again.
lines.why: The sentence that ended my game.

lines.line: Nothing further will happen to you in this game; whoever the old man was waiting for, he has gone to look for them elsewhere.

fun.why: The hooded-figure fight and the unmasking were thrilling, and diving for the amulet was tense. Then the waterlogged lamp turned the last stretch into a series of grue deaths with nothing I could do about it.

engagement.why: I wanted to see every corner, and the blocked exits and the ocean's "yet" kept pulling me on. Losing my light cut that drive short.

difficulty.why: The puzzles were fair, but the lake destroying the only light source with no recovery felt harsh. Death was forgiving until I suddenly ran out of second chances.

interestingness.why: Fighting your own reflection and earning the old man's regalia piece by piece, all against a fallen Empire, is a strong theme. The death visions add to it.

prose.why: The writing is consistently lovely: wry refusals, mournful landscapes, objects with histories.
